The Story of the Brahmin and Alcohol

I bow to the omniscient Lord, the bestower of all happiness, and I write the story of a Brahmin who suffered harm from drinking alcohol, so that all may benefit from reading it.

A ascetic named Pat, a learned scholar of the Vedas and Vedangas, was travelling from Chakrapur to visit the Ganga River. By chance, he entered the Vindhya forest. There, some Chandala youths, maddened by alcohol, were dancing, singing, and indulging in various obscene acts with a woman of their caste. The unfortunate ascetic fell into their hands.

They stopped him and said, "Ah, you have come at just the right time! We were lacking only you. Come, eat meat, drink alcohol, and enjoy this beautiful woman — these are the pleasures of life. Today is a great day of joy for us, and it is rare for great souls like you to come our way. Please fulfil our request."

Hearing this, the poor ascetic was terrified. How could he explain to these drunkards? What could he say that they would understand? He was in great danger. Still, he tried: "Brothers, listen! I am a Brahmin and an ascetic. How can I eat meat or drink alcohol? Please let me go."

The Chandalas said, "Maharaj, whatever you may be, we will not let you go without accepting some offering. We tell you this much — if you eat willingly, it will be good. Otherwise, we will force-feed you. Without accepting our offering, you will not see the Ganga alive."

Now the ascetic was truly frightened. He began to think, and some verses from the smritis came to mind: "A person who eats even a sesame seed's worth of meat will suffer in hell for as long as the sun and moon remain on earth." But the verse also said, "It is the one who eats much meat who truly sins." And regarding alcohol: "Those who drink alcohol made from gooseberries or molasses — that is not considered true alcohol-drinking." And so on.

Using these interpretations, the ascetic rationalised that a small amount would not be a grave sin. He ate a little meat and drank a little alcohol. The Chandalas were pleased and let him go. But the harm was done. The taste of meat and alcohol awakened desires in him that had long been dormant. He found himself thinking about those pleasures again and again. His austerity weakened, his mind became restless, and he gradually fell from his spiritual path.

He abandoned his ascetic life and became a householder, indulging in sensual pleasures. Through the ripening of his sins, he fell into lower births and suffered greatly. Eventually, through the grace of a Jain monk he met in a later life, he regained his human birth, remembered his past folly, and returned to the path of dharma. He practised austerities with great dedication and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even a small amount of intoxicant or forbidden food can awaken dormant desires and lead to a complete fall from the spiritual path. The rationalisations we make in moments of weakness are the tricks of delusion. The wise should strictly avoid all intoxicants and forbidden foods, for they are the gateway to ruin.
